questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Greatest value of a rule written with a square
questions.learningObjective: explain when a rule written with a square has a greatest value
questions.stem: The onboarding note has to explain why a rule written with a square has a greatest value only when the coefficient is negative.

answer.exemplar: In a rule such as y = a(x - h)^2 + k, the squared part is always at least zero, so it can only add to k or take away from it. If a is negative the squared part pushes the output down, so the rule falls away from k in both directions and k is the highest output, reached at the input h. If a is positive the rule rises without bound on either side, so no greatest value exists and the only special point is the least value k. The sign of the coefficient, not the size of the shift, decides which of the two cases applies.

questions.explanation: The squared part of the rule is never negative, so it can only lower the output when the coefficient is negative. A positive coefficient makes the rule grow without bound, which is why the sign alone decides the case.
questions.hint: Compare the sign of the coefficient in front of the square.

answer.exemplar: An equation such as (x - 7)^2 equals 0 asks for an input whose square is zero, and the only number whose square is zero is zero itself, so the base must equal zero and the input is 7. questions.topic: Constant after completing the square
questions.learningObjective: explain why completing the square always lowers the constant
questions.stem: The release notes have to explain why completing the square always changes the constant by a negative amount.

answer.exemplar: Completing the square works by adding the same amount to both sides, and that amount is the square of half the linear coefficient. Adding it to the left is what creates the perfect square, and the same amount taken away from the right keeps the two sides equal, so the constant on the right always falls by a positive number. For y = x^2 + 10x + 6, half of 10 is 5 and the completed form is (x + 5)^2 - 19. A student who adds the 25 instead of subtracting it has changed the rule, moving the turning point and every output with it.

questions.explanation: The square of half the linear coefficient is added on one side and removed on the other, so the constant always falls by that positive amount. Adding it instead would change the rule rather than rewrite it.
questions.hint: The square is gained on one side and paid for on the other.

answer.exemplar: The window is found by finding where the model meets the level, because between two crossings the model is on one side of the level and outside them it is on the other. questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Next table value from a constant second difference
questions.learningObjective: explain why a constant second difference signals a quadratic rule
questions.stem: The explanation for a new engineer has to show why a table with a constant second difference comes from a quadratic rule.

answer.exemplar: A constant second difference is the fingerprint of a quadratic rule, because a rule of the form ax^2 + bx + c changes by a fixed amount each time when the first differences are compared. For the table 4, 9, 16, 25 the first differences are 5, 7 and 9, and the second differences are 2 and 2, so the rule is a quadratic and the next first difference must be 11. That gives the next value 36. A table with a constant first difference is linear instead, and one with no pattern at all is not described by a quadratic, so the second difference must settle before the table is extended.

questions.explanation: A quadratic rule changes by a growing amount, so its first differences grow by a fixed step, and that fixed step is the second difference. A linear table would have a constant first difference instead, and a table with no settled second difference cannot be extended by this method.
questions.hint: Compare the first differences of the first differences.
